strengths: The paper addresses a concrete clinical NLP data-access problem. Synth-SBDH provides 8,767 synthetic examples covering 15 categories with spans, presence, temporal information, and rationales, offering useful coverage beyond the public resources compared in Table 1.

The core utility claim has meaningful empirical support. On MIMIC-SBDH-aligned, prompt-tuned RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro-F. Experiments across model architectures, three-run reporting, and the low-resource results provide evidence that the resource can benefit downstream extraction. This supported contribution merits Findings consideration.

The expert review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples is substantial. Adjudication, corrected annotations, detailed error analysis, generation prompts, all 45 seed examples, and training configurations support scrutiny and reuse. The paper also provides a repository link and reports releasing data and checkpoints.
weaknesses: The claim of consistently improved performance is too broad. In Table 4, RoBERTa NER macro-F slightly decreases, while ClinicalRoBERTa improves only marginally. The largest NER improvement comes from a highly unstable T5 baseline (25.44 ± 18.24 macro-F). Table 14 shows essentially no benefit for larger models. These results support a narrower claim about particular models and data regimes.

The striking rare-category result requires more uncertainty analysis: housing insecurity has only 18 positive test examples. Variation across three training runs does not quantify uncertainty from this small evaluation sample. Class-rebalancing baselines and clearly reported comparisons with equivalent training budgets would also clarify the value of synthetic examples beyond additional training and increased minority-class exposure.

The rationale-distillation claim is preliminary. Table 5 shows absolute macro-F gains of only 0.66 and 0.58 points, with the latter nonsignificant (p = 0.36). Evaluation is confined to synthetic text, and extraction accuracy alone does not establish improved reasoning capability. Real-data extraction evaluation after rationale training would be possible without requiring reference rationales at test time.

The resource's rich annotation schema receives incomplete validation. Synthetic examples average 13.7 words, compared with 35.13 and 47.43 in the real datasets, and the experiments provide no dedicated evaluation of temporal prediction or negation handling. Expert review required 286 updates, 142 discards, and 581 added annotations, indicating substantial label and coverage errors; training annotations remain uncorrected. These limitations constrain claims about comprehensive clinical-text coverage.

Several reporting ambiguities affect reproducibility. Appendix D.2 claims a MIMIC-pretraining comparison, but Table 13 does not clearly distinguish that condition from the ordinary baseline. The reported synthetic split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767, and the deduplication rule says similarity must exceed the threshold with 'all' previous examples, requiring clarification. Access restrictions on VA-SBDH additionally limit independent replication of the real-data NER findings.
